agent.name: Emerging Technology Diffusion Agent
agent.specialty: Diffusion stage, Rogers factors and peer position, and the timing implication for an organization (not the adoption decision)

analytical_question: How far have agentic AI and agent-based applicant support diffused, what is accelerating or inhibiting that diffusion, and what timing implication follows for this organization (without making the adoption decision)?
general_et_finding: Diffusion ladder (evidence date 2026-10-25). L1, generative AI among U.S. adults: early majority, past take-off. 34% of U.S. adults had ever used ChatGPT in Feb-Mar 2025 (D1, grade A), and nearly 40% of adults aged 18-64 used generative AI in late 2024 (D2, A). Microsoft telemetry puts U.S. working-age use at 28.3% in H2 2025 (D3, B; a different measure). Every measure is above the roughly 16% take-off line (C1), but intensity is low: generative AI assisted only 1-5% of work hours (D2). L2a, any AI among U.S. firms: at the take-off line. 19.8% of firms used AI in any business function in the period ending May 2026, within a 17-20% band since December 2025; the rate is 37% for firms with 250+ employees (D4, A; question broadened in November 2025). L2b, agentic AI in organizations: early adopters, before the chasm for production use. No representative measure of agent adoption exists. The Census figure for any AI (D4) is an upper bound for all firms. A self-reported survey of larger firms finds 23% scaling an agent somewhere, but no more than 10% in any given function (D5, B). A self-selected January 2025 poll found 19% with significant agent investment (D7, B). Developers, the lead users, are at 31% (D8, B; not a proxy for other industries). Attention exceeds diffusion: AI agents sat at the Peak of Inflated Expectations in August 2025 (D6), and over 40% of agentic projects are forecast to be cancelled by 2027 (D7). The driver mix is mostly external: vendor launches and standards bodies (D9, D10, D15), with little published peer evidence. Vendor messaging is still 'new' (beta labels, availability disclaimers, D15), not yet 'useful' with referenced results (C1). Accelerators: interoperability standards (MCP, 10,000+ public servers, D9; A2A, 100+ supporting firms, D10); pre-built vendor skills; falling costs. Inhibitors: accuracy and trust (46% of developers distrust AI output, D8); data privacy and security; unclear value. This paragraph is identical for every organization at this evidence date.
application_finding: Application (L3, same for every organization evaluating this application). L3a, FAQ/answer chatbots in admissions and recruitment: past take-off among responding institutions. 36% of marketing, admissions and enrollment respondents use chatbots for FAQs (D11, B, vendor survey, Sept-Nov 2025). Chatbots have been in admissions-adjacent work since the innovator stage around 2016 (D19), at a peer professional-studies school since 2022 (D16), and NYU Admissions described its generative AI admissions bot in November 2025 (D17). L3b, tool-using recruitment agents (the proposed application): innovators/early adopters. The share cannot be measured from current evidence. Vendors offer pre-built recruitment skills, some in beta (D15, C). One named deployment was announced as planned, with a projected, not measured, saving (D14, C). The 2025-26 higher-education surveys report no agent share at all (D11, D12, D13). Five characteristics for L3b against the real baseline (an FAQ chatbot plus staff): relative advantage - Inferred, unproven: the added value is actions (requests, bookings, application starts), but only vendor projections exist (D14). Compatibility - Observed, mixed: the channel already exists (D17, D18), but data security/privacy is the top institutional barrier (56%, D11) and only 9% say privacy policies cover AI (D12). Complexity - Inferred, moderate-high: permissions, CRM integration and human approval. Trialability - Observed, high: pre-built skills and open standards (D9, D10, D15). Observability - Observed, low: no comparable institution has published measured agent outcomes; visible items are announcements and projections (D14, D16). Most important characteristic for timing: observability. Fast followers adopt on visible peer results, and those do not yet exist. That is also why this diffusion is driven by vendors more than by peers. Peer group and organization (L4): professional and continuing-education schools of research universities. Chatbots are established (Syracuse's professional-studies school since 2022, D16). The only survey of this segment is small and self-selected (n=38-58, D13, grade C): 79% expect chatbots to transform enrollment within two years, 36% feel behind peers, and agents are not mentioned. It cannot set a stage. Within NYU: NYU Admissions runs a generative AI bot (D17) and SPS offers the Violet chatbot (D18). SPS is therefore at the implementation stage for FAQ chatbots and at the knowledge/persuasion stage for tool-using agents.
organization_specific_finding: Adopter posture: fast follower (course-case assumption) | Relevant crossing: L3b among comparable professional-education peers | Timing implication: prepare and trial now; no applicant-facing agent launch on diffusion grounds this cycle. A fast follower waits for the application to cross among comparable peers, not for the general public to use generative AI (L1). That crossing has not happened, and peer results are not observable. Trialability is high and the cost of learning is low, so the right timing now is a sandbox trial. The trial is the matched comparison set in Assignments 3-4: staff-only versus Violet or simple retrieval versus the proposed agent, on synthetic or approved inquiries. This keeps SPS ready to move within one cycle once the triggers fire. SPS is not 'late'. It already sits in the early majority for the variant that has crossed (FAQ chatbots), and no peer is visibly ahead on agents. The go/no-go and scale belong to the Adoption specialist. Evidence-quality check: the memo's five claims change none of the above.

evidence.claim: Rogers' adopter categories (2.5/13.5/34/34/16%), five factors, stages, roles; take-off at critical mass of about 16% ('crosses the chasm'); 'Adopt early only if high pay-off in a short time and willing to abandon it'; 'track ... adoption patterns and only adopt after the technology has crossed'; vendor messaging moving from 'This is new' to 'This is useful' signals crossing. Slide 74 frames the team project around NYU SPS and agentic AI recruiting agents.

evidence.evidence_type: commercial online survey, recruitment method not disclosed (grade C)
evidence.notes: Limits: A current or representative adoption rate; agentic recruitment support. Stale (2023), mixed population, undisclosed sampling, and mostly about reviewing documents.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: Memo claim 1 - '82% of colleges use AI in admissions' (D20): grade C, rejected. Stale (2023), mixed population including high schools, undisclosed sampling, and mostly about document review rather than recruitment support or agents. This is the weakest diffusion claim in the case.

Memo claim 2 - '23% are scaling agentic AI, past the 16% chasm' (D5): grade B, rejected as a chasm test. Self-reported respondents from larger firms; scaling 'somewhere' in the organization; no more than 10% in any given function. It cannot be compared with the 16% threshold for admissions offices (denominator rule).

Memo claim 3 - 'UAE 64% shows the U.S. will follow quickly' (D3): rejected. Geographically narrow; measures individuals' generative AI use, not organizations' agents; the U.S. rate in the same report is 28.3%.
Memo claim 4 - '31% of developers use agents, so admissions offices will soon' (D8): rejected. Industry-specific lead users; no transfer to admissions.
Memo claim 5 - '$800 saved per inquiry' (D14): grade C, deferred. A vendor projection for a planned deployment. It cannot rate relative advantage; test it in SPS's own comparison.

Memo conclusion - 'crossed the chasm and SPS is already late': not supported. FAQ chatbots have crossed and NYU already uses them (D17, D18). Tool-using agents have not crossed, and no peer is visibly ahead. With the claims removed, every finding is unchanged.

Weakest diffusion claim: '56% of schools use AI in admissions; 82% by 2024' (D20, grade C). It fails on four counts. It is stale (September 2023). It mixes populations (21% of respondents were private high schools). Its sampling is undisclosed. And it is mostly about reviewing transcripts and letters, not recruitment support or agents. It cannot place L3a or L3b.

Most important evidence gap: there is no representative measure of tool-using agent adoption in higher-education admissions, or of agentic AI in organizations generally. Every agent figure is self-reported, self-selected or vendor-supplied.

Case for an earlier stage than placed: L1 is clearly past take-off, standards are spreading fast (D9, D10), and the large-firm survey reports 23% scaling agents somewhere (D5). Once vendors ship agents inside admissions CRMs by default, L3b could cross quickly. The response to this is monitoring triggers, not an assumed crossing.

Case for a later stage than placed: 'agent' labels are inflated (Gartner judges only about 130 of thousands of vendors real, D7), so even the early-adopter placement for L2b may overstate genuine agent use.
Measures differ across L1 sources (ever used vs. regular use vs. telemetry: D1, D2, D3). They agree only that L1 is past take-off, not on its exact position.
SPS-specific gap: Violet's architecture, usage and vendor roadmap are unknown (D18).
confidence_and_uncertainty: By level. L1 past take-off: High (several A-grade sources agree). L2a at the take-off line: High for the number, Moderate for comparability (the question changed). L2b early adopters: Moderate (no representative agent measure). L3a chatbots past take-off: Moderate (vendor survey). L3b innovators/early adopters: Moderate-Low (based on the absence of evidence; cannot be quantified). L4 peer group: Low (small or anecdotal evidence). Timing implication: Moderate.
value_opportunity_implication: A fast follower can capture most of the learning value cheaply now, because trialability is high. It avoids early-adopter costs: beta features, forecast cancellations (D7) and unproven value. Being trial-ready shortens the lag once peers publish results.
risk_governance_implication: Two timing risks. Moving on attention (D6, D7) could lock SPS into immature tools. Missing the crossing could cost a cycle of catch-up. Governance lags adoption in the sector: only 9% say privacy policies cover AI (D12). Any trial needs approved content, permission limits and staff approval. Legal determinations belong to compliance.
recommendation_management_implication: Treat the next 6-12 months as preparation: run the sandbox comparison, define the measures peers would need to publish, and watch the triggers. Do not schedule an applicant-facing agent pilot on diffusion grounds. Hand to Adoption with this caution: the evidence that people use generative AI, or that vendors sell agents, is not evidence that agent-based applicant support has crossed. Hand to Landscape: check Violet's vendor and whether its roadmap adds agent actions. Reply to the memo: no claim meets the evidence grade needed to move the diffusion stage.
change_monitoring_triggers: Peer observability (owner: this specialist with Landscape, semiannual): at least three comparable institutions publish measured outcomes of tool-using applicant agents (accuracy, response time, staff time, escalations). Compare with today's zero. If met, L3b moves toward crossing and the timing implication moves one step earlier.

Representative measure: a higher-education survey (EDUCAUSE, Ellucian, UPCEA or similar) reports agent use, as distinct from chatbot use, in admissions at 16% or more of institutions. Then treat L3b as past take-off.
Vendor messaging switch (C1): admissions/CRM vendors move recruitment agents from beta to general availability with named customer references and outcomes. That is an earlier timing signal.
Downgrade or hold: rising cancellations, incidents or agent-washing findings (D6, D7 successors), or a flat Census AI-use rate (D4), means keep the current timing or move it later.

Internal (owner: SPS admissions operations): when the sandbox comparison ends, if the agent beats Violet or simple retrieval on accuracy-adjusted cost per inquiry, SPS becomes a candidate opinion leader. Its own published result would raise observability for peers.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: The agent does not decide go/no-go, scale or vendor.
No representative measure of agent adoption in admissions exists, so the L3b share is withheld rather than estimated.
Needed: Violet's design and usage data; how comparable professional-education peers handle agent pilots.
